input.vignette:
A male neonate, aged 2 weeks, is brought to primary care with symptoms of excessive sleepiness, feeding difficulties, and grunting. The infant was delivered at home at approximately 38 weeks gestation without prenatal care. Initially healthy, the infant's condition has gradually deteriorated since birth. The mother, aged 30, reports no significant medical history, hereditary conditions, or drug use during pregnancy. Current vital signs show: temperature 98.6 ºF, blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, heart rate 200/min, and respiratory rate 70/min. Physical examination reveals nasal flaring, costosternal retractions, and perioral cyanosis. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a single S2 and a systolic ejection murmur. The liver is enlarged on abdominal palpation, and all peripheral pulses are bounding. Chest imaging shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vasculature. What is the most likely underlying pathology in this case?

Options:
A. Tetralogy of Fallot
B. Patent ductus arteriosus
C. Double outlet right ventricle
D. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
E. Ebstein anomaly
F. Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection
G. Tricuspid atresia
H. Transposition of the great arteries
I. Atrioventricular septal defect
J. Truncus arteriosus

tachypnea, dyspnea with feeding, poor weight gain, diaphoresis) by age 4 to 6 wk. Pulmonary vascular

obstructive disease (Eisenmenger's syndrome) is usually a late complication but may occur earlier,

especially in children with Down syndrome.

Partial AV septal defects are asymptomatic during childhood if mitral regurgitation is mild or absent.

However, symptoms (eg, exercise intolerance, fatigue, palpitations) may develop during adolescence or

early adulthood. Infants with moderate or severe mitral regurgitation often have signs of HF.

Physical examination in children with complete AV septal defects shows an active precordium due to

volume and pressure overload of the right ventricle; a single, loud 2nd heart sound (S

) due to pulmonary

hypertension; a grade 3 to 4/6 systolic murmur; and sometimes a diastolic murmur at the apex and low left

sternal border. Most children with a partial defect have wide splitting of the S

and a midsystolic (eg,

ejection systolic) murmur audible at the upper left sternal border. A mid-diastolic rumble may be present at

the lower left sternal border when the atrial shunt is large. A cleft in the left AV valve results in a blowing

apical systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation. Thus, cardiac findings in children with the partial form are

the same as those described for secundum ASD (; if mitral regurgitation coexists, there will

also be a high-pitched holosystolic murmur at the apex.

Presentation: This is a male infant, two months and 22 days old, from a non-consanguineous couple and a well-monitored twin pregnancy carried to term by cesarean section. Prenatal ultrasound did not show any anomalies. The mother had gestational diabetes managed with insulin. He was born at 39 weeks of gestation with good adaptation to extra-uterine life. His birth weight was 2.9 kilograms. He was hospitalized on his second day of life in the neonatology unit for 10 days due to early maternal-fetal infection, along with his twin brother who passed away on day 20 of life due to respiratory distress and cyanosis refractory to oxygen. The mother reported episodes of cyanosis during exertion (such as crying or feeding) observed since birth. However, no signs of fatigue or sweating during feedings were reported. The baby was admitted with respiratory distress characterized by rapid breathing, cough, and nasal congestion, with a decrease in feeding frequency evolving one week before admission, in the absence of fever. On admission, he was tonic, responsive, and smiling, with a normal weight of 4kg 900gms. He had refractory cyanosis on the hyperoxia test, with a saturation of 78% on room air and 84% on. Confirmed diagnosis: Total Intracardiac Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return and Tetralogy of Fallot. Differential diagnosis includes: Total Intracardiac Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return and Tetralogy of Fallot.

tissue oxygenation. Patients with a large VSD, a patent ductus arteriosus, or both are less cyanotic, but

absent unless associated anomalies are present. The 2nd heart sound (S

Presentation: A 10-day-old male neonate, weighing 3700 g at birth, firstborn of non-relative parents, delivered via cesarean section at 40 weeks gestation with a good Apgar score, was referred to the pediatric emergency department of Motahari hospital of Urmia. The mother reported that the baby had shortness of breath, rapid breathing, and vomiting. The neonate had been admitted to the NICU on the 2nd day after birth due to dehydration and poor feeding on the 1st day. The baby had not been able to take sufficient oral feeding for the past 2 days, and vomiting had worsened. Vital signs were: PR: 162/min, RR: 62/min, BT: 36.5°C, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. The mucous membranes were dry, but skin turgor and fontanels were normal. The chest was normal and symmetric with subcostal retraction and tachypnea. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade II/VI continuous murmur. Peripheral pulses were palpable. Abdominal examination showed an increased liver span on palpation and generalized edema. Primitive neonatal ref. Confirmed diagnosis: Hemitruncus Arteriosus. Differential diagnosis includes: Hemitruncus Arteriosus.

Presentation: A 23-year-old female presented with persistent diarrhea since early infancy, unresponsive to semi-elemental formula. At age 6, she was referred to gastroenterology for ongoing non-bloody diarrhea, with growth parameters below the 5th percentile. Laboratory results showed tissue transglutaminase (TTG) IgA > 142 EU/ml and endomysial antibody (EMA) 1:640. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed absent duodenal villi and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes on histopathology. She was placed on a strict gluten-free diet (GFD). Histopathology findings were consistent with celiac disease. The colon appeared normal on mul. Confirmed diagnosis: CTLA4 haploinsufficiency. Differential diagnosis includes: CTLA4 haploinsufficiency.

On day 10, during a routine visit, a grade 3/6 systolic murmur was detected, leading to a referral to a cardiologist. On day 14, the cardiologist noted a h. Confirmed diagnosis: Tetralogy of Fallot with absent left pulmonary artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Tetralogy of Fallot with absent left pulmonary artery.
